preamble: The shift from the voiceless alveolar stop [t] to its voiced counterpart [d] is a primary form of lenition. It typically occurs in intervocalic positions where the vocal folds continue to vibrate through the consonant, assimilating the stop to the surrounding vowels.

examples.note: Latin intervocalic [t] voices to [d] in Spanish.
French historical voicing [t] > [d], then further lenition and elision.
Intervocalic flapping/voicing: /t/ becomes a voiced alveolar tap.
Consonant gradation weak grade: word-medial /t/ voices to [d] in closed syllable context (nominative vs. oblique).
Systematic intervocalic voicing in weak grade of consonant gradation paradigm.
Intervocalic voicing: /t/ is realized as [d] between voiced sounds.

Morphologically conditioned intervocalic voicing in Nuer: morpheme-final /t/ is voiced to [d] in intervocalic position before a vowel-initial suffix. This voicing alternation is restricted to morpheme-final consonants — the same consonant in suffix-initial position does not undergo the change. Dental articulation [t̪, d̪] is common before front vowels.

Dinka verb morphology uses stem-internal consonant voicing alternations alongside vowel changes. Stop voicing alternations in stem-final position interact with the ATR-based vowel harmony system, with voiced obstruents co-occurring with [+ATR] vowels in certain morphological paradigms.
Initial t- voiced in Oghuz; Kazakh and Uzbek keep t-.
Dahl's law: a voiceless stop voices when the next syllable also begins with a voiceless stop; cf. Swahili -tatu, which lacks the law
lenis *t is voiced; cf. Valley Zapotec zedəꞌ
PMP *t became Palauan d, which is often realized as the fricative [ð].
All stops became voiced in non-final syllables; Copala takãã and Itunyoso takã keep t.
